clips.title: What is the Critical Path Method (CPM)?
clips.why: A project manager explains, step by step, how to find the chain of tasks that decides when a project can finish, which is exactly what you do with the pilot ticket.
look: The steps: list the tasks, put them in order of what depends on what, give each a duration, then find the longest chain.
Float: a task that is not on the critical path can slip a little without moving the end date.
Why a late task on the critical path moves the whole project.
clips.after: The deps of our tickets are the arrows in his diagram. The chain from the walls through the runtime to the pilot is our critical path, which is why a late wall moves the pilot date.

clips.title: Coding is no longer the constraint: Scaling devex to teams and agents at Spotify
clips.why: Spotify's chief architect describes the code-maintenance automation they ran before any AI agent, which is the system their agent was later added to.
look: What kind of maintenance work Spotify automated across many repos before agents existed.
How much easier it is to add an agent to a process that is already automated and trusted.
clips.after: Our plan works the same way: Renovate, fast tests and the brain's pages start before Nova, so the agents arrive in a place that is already organised.

clips.title: Coding is no longer the constraint: Scaling devex to teams and agents at Spotify
clips.why: The same talk, on quality and guardrails: why firm rules around agents make a team faster instead of slower.
look: His argument that firm guardrails make teams faster, not slower.
What kinds of checks keep agent changes safe to merge.
clips.after: That is one reason our walls come first in the plan: when the guardrails exist from the start, nobody has to stop Nova later to add them.

practice.q: Put these milestones of the quarter in the order the plan builds them.
items: The walls: the agents' GitHub App, the gateway and the independent-approval check
The runtime: account, network, warm machines, broker and harness
Nova's workflow: plan, approval, build, questions and PR
The failure drills, run with Security
Nova works on tickets of its own platform repo
The pilot: the first small product tickets go to Nova
practice.why: Each layer needs the one before it. The drills and the work on its own repo come before the product pilot, so Nova is proven where a mistake costs least.

practice.q: A ticket's deps list holds one key from its own goal, and its needs says "G0: the rhino-ai-agents GitHub App and its private key in Vault." What do the two fields tell you?

options.text: It waits for one ticket of its own goal, and it also needs the GitHub App from the walls goal.
options.why: deps points inside the same goal with keys. needs describes in words what must come from another goal.

options.text: It waits for two tickets, both in its own goal.
options.why: needs is not a list of keys in the same goal. Here it names something from G0.

options.text: needs is only a comment; only deps decides the order.
options.why: needs is real order too. It is written as text because it crosses goals, so a person has to read it.

practice.q: In timeline.mjs, a ticket is planned in a week when the week is between its first and last week. Fill in the index.
practice.hint: w is a pair: [first week, last week].
practice.why: w[0] is the first week and w[1] the last, so [9, 10] means the work happens in weeks 9 and 10.

practice.q: You are in the frontend guild. When does the plan first need your hands?

options.text: Only from week 9, when Nova's pull requests arrive for review.
options.why: Reviewing Nova's PRs is the last guild task, not the first.

options.text: In weeks 3 to 5, labelling real past bugs so Byte's reviews can be measured.
options.why: The gold set for Byte is the guilds' first work. Brain pages, skills and npm run verify follow in weeks 5 to 7.

options.text: Never: the platform team does all of it.
options.why: The guilds own 15 tickets, because only they know which bugs were real and what a good skill for their area says.

practice.q: Why does Nova get TICKET-BENCH, a set of past tickets with hidden tests, before the pilot starts?

options.text: So Nova has a score before people depend on it, and every later change can be compared with that score.
options.why: Measure first, then trust. A bench tells you whether a change made Nova better or worse, without waiting for real tickets.

options.text: So Nova can practise on the tickets and remember the answers.
options.why: The tests are hidden from Nova on purpose. A bench it could memorise would measure nothing.

options.text: Because the product team needs those old tickets done again.
options.why: The tickets are already done. They are reused only because their correct answers are known.

practice.q: A ticket is flagged stretch. What does that mean?

options.text: It is blocked on another team.
options.why: Blocking shows in deps and needs, not in the flag.

options.text: It is a decision with an owner, usually a meeting with no code.
It is useful work we do only if there is time left in the quarter.
options.why: Nine tickets are stretch. Nothing else in the plan waits for them.
